AKM Shamsuddin and others ----- Plaintiff-Appellants
Vs.

full_judgment:
ATM Afzal J: This appeal by the plaintiffs, following leave, arises out of a suit, Title Suit No. 432 of 1983, for ejectment of the defendant-respondent, a monthly tenant, from the suit premises and is directed against the judgment and order dated 1st April, 1987 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division (Jessore Session) in Civil Revision No. 246 of 1986 making the Rule absolute and dismissing the suit upon setting aside the concurrent decision of the Courts below. 

 2. Plaintiffs instituted the aforesaid suit in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Sadar Upazila, Kushtia on the averments, inter alia, that the suit premises belonged to one Abdus Sattar and the plaintiffs purchased the same along with other properties for valuable consideration by four registered kabalas dated 24.11.79 after publication in the local weekly 'Ispat' dated 25.8.79 that the defendant was an ejectable monthly tenant under the plaintiff's predecessor at a monthly rental of Tk. 68.00; that at the time of the kabala the vendor introduced the plaintiffs to the defendant as the new owner of the suit premises; that the defendant is a worst defaulter, he did not clear rent in time to the plaintiffs' predecessor and since purchase, in spite of reported request, did not care to pay rent to the plaintiffs for the period from 1.11.79 to date, that is, 31.8.83; that the plaintiffs are all businessmen and they are in bonafide need of the suit premises for their own use and occupation for business purpose; that the defendant has got his own suitable premises at HSS Road and at other commercial places in the town which he may use for his own purpose and that the plaintiffs served notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act upon the defendant on 31.5.83 which was received by the defendant on 8.6.83 but he did not vacate the suit premises after 31.8.83 as demanded. The plaintiffs filed the suit on 25.9.83. 

 3. Defendant-respondent contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the averments made by the plaintiffs and further asserting, inter alia, that he is a respectable physician, he carries on his profession and the business of medicine in the suit premises and it is the only source of his income; that the plaintiffs' predecessor and the plaintiffs refused to accept the present rent and further the plaintiffs demanded Tk. 20,000.00 from the defendant as salami whereupon he was compelled to deposit rent with the Rent Controller in Misc. Case No. 202 of 1982 and that the suit was barred, among others, by the principle of res judicata as the previous Title Suit No. 22 of 1982 was dismissed. 

 5. On appeal by the defendant against the said decree, Title Appeal No. 142 of 1984, the learned Subordinate Judge, Kushtia dismissed the same by his judgment and decree dated 10 August, 1986. The defendant then took a revision, Civil Revision No. 246 of 1986, to the High Court Division and, as already noticed, the concurrent decision of the Courts below was reversed and the suit dismissed by the impugned judgment. 

 6. Leave was granted to consider mainly whether the learned Judge of the High Court Division upon a correct appreciation of the facts of the case and the law, particularly sections 18(5) and 19(1)(a)(b) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 (Ordinance XX of 1963), briefly the Ordinance, rightly held that the defendant "was not a defaulter in payment of rent at any point of time" and as such the courts below committed error of law in decreeing the suit. 

 7. As far as the law is concerned it has been authoritatively laid down in the case of Ramjan Ali Mistry 31 DLR (AD)183 that in terms of the aforesaid sections the protection of the tenant against ejectment is on the fulfillment of certain conditions. "The tenant must pay rent in terms of the contract, and in the absence of the contract within fifteenth day next following month on which the rent falls due, and if the landlord refuses to accept the rent tendered by the tenant, the tenant must remit the rent within the aforesaid fifteenth day of the following month by money order. If the rent remitted by money order is refused, the tenant can deposit the rent with the Rent Controller within a fortnight from the date of the receipt of the undelivered rent sent through the postal authority, and when these conditions as prescribed in the Ordinance are fulfilled by the tenant he gets the protection, otherwise the protection from ejectment on ground of default in the payment of rent granted by the Ordinance is clearly taken away by the express language of sub-section (5) of section 18." 

 8. It will be seen that the plaintiffs' case is that the defendant failed to pay rent ever since their purchase of the suit premises from Abdus Sattar by Kabalas dated 24.11.79 and 28.11.79 even though the defendant was introduced to the plaintiffs at the time of the kabalas by Abdus Sattar and asked to pay rent to them (plaintiffs) henceforth. Defendant took the plea that on their refusal to accept the rent, he had been depositing the same with the House Rent Controller, firstly, in the name of Abdus Sattar and then coming to know of the transfer in favour of the plaintiffs, in the name of the plaintiffs. The trial Court found from the record of Misc. Case No. 280/80 that the defendant had been depositing rent in favour of Abdus Sattar since September, 1980 up to July, 1982. Defendant stated that he came to know on 7.9.82 that the plaintiffs had purchased the suit premises. Then he filed Misc. Case No. 202/82 and has been depositing rent with the Rent Controller regularly in favour of the plaintiffs since 22.9.82. 

 9. In order that the deposit made by the tenant under section 19 of the Ordinance can be treated as validly made, the pre-condition is that the tenant must first offer the rent to the landlord in time and if the landlord refuses to accept the rent tendered by the tenant, he must remit the rent by postal money order within the stipulated time and only on refusal of the landlord to accept such remittance, the tenant may deposit rent under section 19(1)(a). The 'Explanation' to section 18(5) clearly says that "a landlord shall not for the purposes of this sub-section be deemed to have refused to accept any rent unless the rent is remitted within the period referred to above in this sub-section by postal money order ") 

 10. The law has been clearly laid down in the other case of Abul Layes 29 DLR (SC) 13 that it is incumbent upon the tenant to pay rent directly to the landlord and it is only on the contingencies specified in section 19 that the tenant may deposit rent with the Rent Controller and as such when a tenant elects to resort to the said provisions of section 19 the onus is on him to prove that the ground on which he deposited the rent with the Rent Controller exists. 

 11. Now in the present case there is absolutely no evidence that the defendant ever offered any rent or sent the same by money order to the plaintiffs before making the deposit in their names in Misc. Case No. 202/82. In the written statement it has merely been stated that the plaintiffs' predecessor and the plaintiffs refused to accept the present rent and they demanded too high rent of the suit premises for which the defendant has been compelled to deposit the rent in the Court in Misc. Case No. 202/82. There is no mention even that the rent was sent by money order. The only witness for the defendant, he himself, said nothing about remitting any rent to the plaintiffs before making the deposit in their names. The deposit thus made does not, therefore. qualify to be a valid tender of rent and consequently cannot save the tenant from being a defaulter and the liability for eviction. 

 12. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, learned counsel for the defendant-respondent, has argued that the plaintiffs have not raised any issue as to the sending of rent by money order and there being no dispute that the rent is being deposited in the name of the plaintiffs in Misc. Case No. 202/82, it must be presumed that the proceedings there have been regularly taken, that is, the deposit must have been made after remittance of the rent by money order. It is difficult to accept the submission of Mr. Hossain because of the heavy burden that lies upon the tenant to discharge. The onus is upon the tenant to prove that the conditions for depositing the rent with the Rent Controller were satisfied. It is not enough to prove that the rent was deposited under section 19 without further proof that the tenant was legally entitled to make the deposit. There cannot be any presumption as to due offer of rent to the landlord nor the landlord is required to raise the issue of money order, etc. As stated in the 29 DLR (SC) 13 case, no duty under the law has been cast upon the landlord to pursue the tenant in demanding the rent which falls due. It is rather the duty of the tenant to pay rent to the landlord in time with a view to saving him from being a defaulter, the consequence of which is his eviction from the premises in his occupation. 

 13. The courts below in the present case specifically found that the defendant had defaulted in making the deposit of rent in time for the months of September and December, 1983. The learned Judge of the High Court Division, however, found that the said deposits were made within time. The learned Judge observed that the Courts below had not found any default in payment of rent for any particular or specific month before filing of the suit on 25.9.83. "On the other hand, it appears" the impugned judgment says, "that the defendant had been depositing rents in the Court of the House Rent Controller   from the month of September 1980 till the filing of the suit on 25.9.83. As such the plaintiffs failed to prove any default of payment of rent before filing the suit on 25.9.83. So, in my view, there was no cause of action before filing TS No. 432 of 1983 on 25.9.83." 

 14. From the above it is clear that the learned Judge upon a misconception of the legal provisions and a failure to correctly perceive the principles laid down in the decisions referred to above completely failed to consider whether the deposits made by the defendant could legally be held to be valid deposits which can afford him protection from eviction. It has already been shown that the deposits not having been made in compliance with sections 18 and 19 of the Ordinance, i.e. without first offering and then remitting the rent by postal money order, the defendant remained a defaulter and as such liable for eviction. 

 15. The learned Judge of the High Court Division was not also right in finding that the courts below had not found any default in payment of rent before the filing of the suit on 25.9.83. Had the judgment of the trial Court been carefully read, it should have been found that the case of the plaintiffs that there was default made by the defendant right from November, 1979 inasmuch as he failed to pay rent to the plaintiffs even though he was introduced to them by the plaintiff vendors' Abdus Sattar, was fully accepted. If the plaintiffs were introduced to the defendant in November, 1979, the deposit of rent thereafter in the name of the plaintiff vendors' Abdus Sattar could not be treated as a valid deposit. In the case of Basiruddin Ahmed 36 DLR (AD) 191 it has been held that "deposit of rent in favour of the previous landlord became totally irrelevant as soon as that landlord ceased to have any interest in the suit premises after the transfer; deposit in her favour cannot be taken as a ground to resist ejectment when sought by the new landlord to whom no rent was paid in spite of the notice of the transfer". The learned Judge of the High Court Division regrettably lost sight of the findings of fact made by the Court below and the principle just referred to in the matter of deposit. The trial Court, it must be said, made a much better appreciation of both fact and law which has evidently escaped the notice of the learned Judge of the High Court Division. 

 16. The learned Assistant Judge observed in his judgment; "Plaintiffs purchased the suit premises on 24.11.79 and 28.11.79. It is not believable at all that they were not introduced within this long period from 24.11.79 to July/82 and they (plaintiff) did not claim rent from the defendant. I think that the defendant intentionally suppressed the fact that he had been depositing rent in favour of PW 2 though he was not his landlord at that time." Further, "It is true that if the landlord refuses to accept the rent, the tenant has a right to deposit it with the Rent Controller but it must be deposited within the stipulated time in accordance with the provisions of sections 18 and 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. If it is not so paid or deposited the defaulter cannot get the protection of law by depositing the rent with the rent controller subsequently, a tenant not having paid the rent to the landlord in terms of section 18(5) nor having deposited the same with the Rent Controller, according to section 19 is not entitled to claim protection from eviction. Defendant of this suit cannot claim protection from eviction from the Court as he has been proved a defaulter. 

 17. It appears that the learned Judge of the High Court Division accepted the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the defendant that there was no default in payment of rent by the defendant because under Misc. Case No. 280/80 the defendant deposited rent in favour of the previous landlord from September, 1980 to July 1982 and thereafter under Misc Case No. 202/82 he started depositing in favour of the plaintiffs since August, 1982 and since then has been depositing the rent regularly. The question which should have been asked by the learned Judge of the High Court Division is whether in view of the findings of the Courts below and the provisions of law, the alleged deposits made by the defendant were in accordance with the terms of the Ordinance. From the impugned judgment it is not to be found that the question as above at all occurred to the learned Judge but even then it was found that the defendant was not a defaulter in payment of rent at any point of time, From the reasons already indicated it must be said that the learned Judge was wholly wrong in making the said finding. 

 18. Deposit made in favour of the plaintiffs' vendor knowing that the suit premises was already transferred to the plaintiff was not a valid deposit. In repelling this contention the learned judge referred to the fact that the earlier suit for eviction, TS No. 22 of 1982, was dismissed for default on 30.10.82 and, therefore, it was held that the old grievance could not be agitated in the present suit. It must be said that this was a wrong view because in the present suit, started on a fresh cause of action, the court is bound to consider whether the deposit made in favour of the former landlord was a valid deposit. Then again the learned Judge without reference to the evidence and the findings of the courts below wrongly held that the plaintiffs failed to prove the knowledge of the defendant as to the transfer of the premises in question (before July 1982). PW 1 AMM Shamsuddin (Plaintiff) and PW 2 Abdus Sattar (vendor of the Plaintiffs) corroborated each other that at the time of kabala the defendant was introduced to the plaintiffs and asked to pay rent to them. As against such evidence there is the denial only of the defendant. Mr. Asrarul Hossain submitted that the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 was discrepant on the point, because, whereas PW 1 said in cross-examination that he was introduced (to the defendant) 1/2 days before the sale, PW 2 said that the introduction was made just after the sale. This is not a material contradiction and further the finding of the trial Court is positive that it is unbelievable that the parties were not introduced within the long period from 24.11.79 to July, 1982. In any case, the learned Judge was wrong in not following 36 DLR (AD) 191 in the facts of the present case. 

 19. Even ignoring the question of deposit in favour of the former landlord, the very fact that rent was being deposited in the name of the plaintiffs since 22.9.82 (in Misc Case No. 202/82) without tendering the same to the plaintiffs first and then remitting it by money order brings the defendant within the mischief of non-compliance of the provisions of sections 18(5) and 19(1)(a) of the Ordinance.
